title: Interface Composition
story: A library needs to handle documents that can be both read AND written. Some documents are read-only, some are write-only, and some support both. How do you express 'a type must satisfy BOTH interfaces' without creating a monster single interface? Interface composition.
why: Interface composition lets you require multiple capabilities from a type by combining interfaces with +, keeping each interface small and focused.
analogy: A Swiss Army knife has separate tools - a blade, scissors, screwdriver. You don't make one giant 'does-everything' tool. You just pick up the knife when you need multiple capabilities. Interface composition is the same: implement small interfaces separately, combine them with + when needed.
try_it: Create two more types that implement Readable and Writable (e.g., Whiteboard and Journal). Then create a function `backup[T: Readable]` that reads and prints content. Pass all three types to backup to see polymorphism in action.
tips: Use `T: A + B` to require multiple interfaces - this is 'interface composition'
Each interface should be small and focused - don't cram unrelated methods together
A type can implement any number of interfaces independently
common_mistakes: Trying to combine interfaces by making one giant interface - use + instead
Forgetting to put the type parameter name: `fn f[T: A + B]` not `fn f[A + B]`
Confusing interface composition (+) with multiple type parameters: `[T: A, U: B]` is different
